claim: Metazoan proteomes contain many paralogous proteins that have evolved distinct functions.
source: Metazoan proteomes contain many paralogous proteins that have evolved distinct functions.
evidence: This is a general statement about metazoan proteomes supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: The Ena/VASP family of actin regulators consists of three members that share an EVH1 interaction domain with a 100% conserved binding site.
source: The Ena/VASP family of actin regulators consists of three members that share an EVH1 interaction domain with a 100 % conserved binding site.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1A and structural data in Figure 1B showing 100% conservation of the FP4-binding site.

claim: A proteome-wide screen revealed photoreceptor cilium actin regulator (PCARE) as a high-affinity ligand for ENAH EVH1.
source: A proteome-wide screen revealed photoreceptor cilium actin regulator (PCARE) as a high-affinity ligand for ENAH EVH1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from a proteomic screen described in the manuscript and referenced in the Results section.

claim: PCARE is ~100-fold specific for ENAH over paralogs VASP and EVL.
source: PCARE is ~100-fold specific for ENAH over paralogs VASP and EVL
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating 70- to 140-fold preference.

claim: PCARE can selectively bind ENAH and inhibit ENAH-dependent adhesion in cells.
source: PCARE is ~100-fold specific for ENAH over paralogs VASP and EVL and can selectively bind ENAH and inhibit ENAH-dependent adhesion in cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell-based experiments shown in Figure 2 demonstrating selective binding and effects on adhesion.

claim: Specificity arises from a mechanism whereby PCARE stabilizes a conformation of the ENAH EVH1 domain that is inaccessible to family members VASP and EVL.
source: Specificity arises from a mechanism whereby PCARE stabilizes a conformation of the ENAH EVH1 domain that is inaccessible to family members VASP and EVL.
evidence: This is supported by structural data (Figure 3, Figure 4) and mutagenesis experiments (Table 1) showing conformational differences.

claim: Structure-based modeling rapidly identified seven residues distributed throughout EVL that are sufficient to differentiate binding by ENAH vs. EVL.
source: Structure-based modeling rapidly identified seven residues distributed throughout EVL that are sufficient to differentiate binding by ENAH vs. EVL.
evidence: This is supported by dTERMen modeling results shown in Figure 4B and experimental validation in Figure 4C.

claim: The authors rationally designed the tightest and most selective ENAH binder to date by exploiting the ENAH-specific conformation.
source: By exploiting the ENAH-specific conformation, we rationally designed the tightest and most selective ENAH binder to date.
evidence: This is supported by binding data for PCARE-Dual shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The Ena/VASP proteins are a family of actin regulators involved in functions ranging from T-cell activation to axon guidance.
source: The Ena/VASP proteins are a family of actin regulators involved in functions ranging from T-cell activation to axon guidance (Kwiatkowski et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: There are three paralogs in mammals: ENAH (often called Mena), VASP, and EVL.
source: There are three paralogs in mammals: ENAH (often called Mena), VASP, and EVL.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Ena/VASP family.

claim: All three Ena/VASP proteins contain an N-terminal EVH1 interaction domain responsible for subcellular localization and a C-terminal EVH2 domain that polymerizes actin.
source: All three proteins contain an N-terminal EVH1 interaction domain responsible for subcellular localization and a C-terminal EVH2 domain that polymerizes actin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ena/VASP protein structure and function.

claim: The two domains are connected by a linker, predicted to be largely disordered, that contains binding motifs for other proteins.
source: The two domains are connected by a linker, predicted to be largely disordered, that contains binding motifs for other proteins.
evidence: This is based on structural predictions and established knowledge about Ena/VASP proteins.

claim: The EVH1 domain binds SLiMs with the consensus motif [FWYL]PXΦP, where X is any amino acid and Φ is any hydrophobic residue.
source: The EVH1 domain binds SLiMs with the consensus motif [FWYL]PXΦP, where X is any amino acid and Φ is any hydrophobic residue (Ball et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The FP4 motif binds the EVH1 domain as a polyproline type II (PPII) helix.
source: This sequence, referred to here as the FP4 motif, binds the EVH1 domain as a polyproline type II (PPII) helix.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FP4 motif binding mode.

claim: ENAH, VASP, and EVL can all bind to FP4 motifs in lamellipodin to promote actin assembly at the leading edge.
source: On the one hand, ENAH, VASP, and EVL can all bind to FP4 motifs in lamellipodin to promote actin assembly at the leading edge (Krause et al., 2004; Hansen and Mullins, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Single deletions of Ena/VASP paralogs lead to mild phenotypic defects in mice, indicating that the paralogs can functionally compensate for each other.
source: Single deletions of Ena/VASP paralogs lead to mild phenotypic defects in mice, indicating that the paralogs can functionally compensate for each other, whereas triple mutant mice die after proceeding to late embryogenesis (Aszódi et al., 1999; Lanier et al., 1999; Kwiatkowski et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature describing mouse genetic studies.

claim: Triple mutant mice die after proceeding to late embryogenesis.
source: Single deletions of Ena/VASP paralogs lead to mild phenotypic defects in mice, indicating that the paralogs can functionally compensate for each other, whereas triple mutant mice die after proceeding to late embryogenesis (Aszódi et al., 1999; Lanier et al., 1999; Kwiatkowski et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature describing mouse genetic studies.

claim: ENAH, alone, promotes haptotaxis of breast cancer cells through fibronectin gradients.
source: ENAH, alone, promotes haptotaxis of breast cancer cells through fibronectin gradients and regulates translation of specific mRNAs in developing axons, implicating it in functions beyond its role in actin polymerization (Oudin et al., 2016; Vidaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ENAH regulates translation of specific mRNAs in developing axons, implicating it in functions beyond its role in actin polymerization.
source: ENAH, alone, promotes haptotaxis of breast cancer cells through fibronectin gradients and regulates translation of specific mRNAs in developing axons, implicating it in functions beyond its role in actin polymerization (Oudin et al., 2016; Vidaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ENAH and VASP promote the invasive potential of migratory breast cancer cells.
source: In addition, whereas ENAH and VASP promote the invasive potential of migratory breast cancer cells, EVL suppresses breast cancer invasion (Roussos et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2009; Padilla-Rodriguez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: EVL suppresses breast cancer invasion.
source: In addition, whereas ENAH and VASP promote the invasive potential of migratory breast cancer cells, EVL suppresses breast cancer invasion (Roussos et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2009; Padilla-Rodriguez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The FP4-binding pocket of the EVH1 domain is 100% conserved across ENAH, VASP, and EVL.
source: The FP4-binding pocket of the EVH1 domain is 100 % conserved across ENAH, VASP, and EVL, and the paralogs share 62–72% sequence identity over the entire domain (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1A and structural representation in Figure 1B.

claim: The Ena/VASP paralogs share 62–72% sequence identity over the entire EVH1 domain.
source: The FP4-binding pocket of the EVH1 domain is 100 % conserved across ENAH, VASP, and EVL, and the paralogs share 62–72% sequence identity over the entire domain (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The three EVH1 domains recognize many common binding partners.
source: Consequently, the three EVH1 domains recognize many common binding partners.
evidence: This is inferred from the high conservation of the binding site and supported by established knowledge.

claim: The LIM3 domain of testin binds specifically to the ENAH EVH1 domain in a region adjacent to the highly conserved FP4-binding pocket.
source: The LIM3 domain of testin binds specifically to the ENAH EVH1 domain in a region adjacent to the highly conserved FP4-binding pocket; this is the only example of an endogenous Ena/VASP EVH1-binding partner where the mechanistic basis for specificity is defined (Boëda et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Testin is the only example of an endogenous Ena/VASP EVH1-binding partner where the mechanistic basis for specificity is defined.
source: The LIM3 domain of testin binds specifically to the ENAH EVH1 domain in a region adjacent to the highly conserved FP4-binding pocket; this is the only example of an endogenous Ena/VASP EVH1-binding partner where the mechanistic basis for specificity is defined (Boëda et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature and knowledge of the field.

claim: Testin binds specifically because it contacts residues that have diverged across paralogs to form distinct surfaces.
source: Testin binds specifically because it contacts residues that have diverged across paralogs to form distinct surfaces, which is a common mechanism for achieving specificity (Skerker et al., 2008; Bardwell et al., 2009; Schreiber and Keating, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A 36-residue peptide from PCARE (PCARE813–848) bound to ENAH with a KD of 0.19 μM.
source: The highest affinity hit from our screen was a 36-residue peptide from PCARE (PCARE813–848) that bound to ENAH with a KD of 0.19 μM (Hwang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from a proteomic screen and cited in a prior publication.

claim: 23-residue PCARE826–848 (PCARE B) maintains high affinity for ENAH EVH1 (KD = 0.32 μM).
source: Truncation studies showed that 23-residue PCARE826–848, which we call PCARE B, maintains high affinity for ENAH EVH1 (KD = 0.32 μM).
evidence: This is supported by experimental truncation studies and binding measurements.

claim: PCARE B exhibits a 70- to 140-fold preference for binding to ENAH over EVL or VASP.
source: To explore the paralog specificity of PCARE B, we quantified binding to EVL and VASP EVH1 domains using biolayer interferometry (BLI) and discovered a 70- to 140-fold preference for binding to ENAH over EVL or VASP (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PCARE is almost exclusively expressed in the retina.
source: PCARE is almost exclusively expressed in the retina, and mutations in PCARE are associated with inherited retinitis pigmentosa and retinal dystrophy (Collin et al., 2010; Nishimura et al., 2010; Kevany et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mutations in PCARE are associated with inherited retinitis pigmentosa and retinal dystrophy.
source: PCARE is almost exclusively expressed in the retina, and mutations in PCARE are associated with inherited retinitis pigmentosa and retinal dystrophy (Collin et al., 2010; Nishimura et al., 2010; Kevany et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Prior work implicates PCARE as a scaffold protein important for recruiting complexes that regulate actin assembly as part of new outer segment disk formation in photoreceptor cells.
source: Prior work implicates PCARE as a scaffold protein important for recruiting complexes that regulate actin assembly as part of new outer segment disk formation in photoreceptor cells (Corral-Serrano et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Previous investigations identified ENAH as an interaction partner for PCARE based on tandem-affinity purification experiments in HEK293T cells.
source: Previous investigations identified ENAH as an interaction partner for PCARE based on tandem-affinity purification experiments in HEK293T cells and colocalization of PCARE with Ena/VASP at ciliary membrane expansions in hTERT RPE1 cells (Boldt et al., 2016; Corral-Serrano et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PCARE colocalizes with Ena/VASP at ciliary membrane expansions in hTERT RPE1 cells.
source: Previous investigations identified ENAH as an interaction partner for PCARE based on tandem-affinity purification experiments in HEK293T cells and colocalization of PCARE with Ena/VASP at ciliary membrane expansions in hTERT RPE1 cells (Boldt et al., 2016; Corral-Serrano et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PCARE was associated with 17 other proteins with actin-related functions via protein tandem-affinity purification studies.
source: PCARE was also associated, via protein tandem-affinity purification studies, with 17 other proteins with actin-related functions, including Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome protein family member 3 (WASF3), which is recruited via PCARE to the cilium, leading to membrane expansions that involve actin polymerization (Corral-Serrano et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: WASF3 is recruited via PCARE to the cilium, leading to membrane expansions that involve actin polymerization.
source: PCARE was also associated, via protein tandem-affinity purification studies, with 17 other proteins with actin-related functions, including Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome protein family member 3 (WASF3), which is recruited via PCARE to the cilium, leading to membrane expansions that involve actin polymerization (Corral-Serrano et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: mRuby2-PCARE B was moderately enriched at focal adhesions when coexpressed with ENAH.
source: mRuby2-PCARE B exhibited diffuse cytoplasmic localization under all conditions except when coexpressed with ENAH, in which case mRuby2-PCARE B was moderately enriched at focal adhesions, consistent with an ENAH–PCARE B interaction (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is significant enrichment (p < 0.0001) of mRuby2-PCARE B with GFP-ENAH at focal adhesions compared to the cytoplasm.
source: We observed significant enrichment (p < 0.0001) of mRuby2-PCARE B with GFP-ENAH at focal adhesions compared to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The enrichment ratios for mRuby2-PCARE B with GFP-EVL and GFP-VASP were not significant.
source: The enrichment ratios for mRuby2-PCARE B with GFP-EVL and GFP-VASP were not significant (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ENAH was significantly colocalized with Mito-mRuby2-PCARE B at mitochondria.
source: In MVD7shEVL cells with exogenously expressed Ena/VASP paralogs, ENAH was significantly colocalized with Mito-mRuby2-PCARE B at mitochondria, although some ENAH remained associated with focal adhesions.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: EVL and VASP remained entirely localized to focal adhesions and did not localize to mitochondria when Mito-mRuby2-PCARE B was expressed.
source: In contrast, EVL and VASP remained entirely localized to focal adhesions and did not localize to mitochondria (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: There is significant enrichment (p < 0.0001) of Mito-mRuby2-PCARE B with GFP-ENAH at the mitochondria compared to the cytoplasm.
source: There is significant enrichment (p < 0.0001) of Mito-mRuby2-PCARE B with GFP-ENAH at the mitochondria compared to the cytoplasm, whereas the enrichment ratios of Mito-mRuby2-PCARE B with GFP-EVL and GFP-VASP were not significant (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ENAH knockdown was associated with diminished adhesion and smaller focal adhesion size compared to cells expressing nontargeting shRNA.
source: As expected, ENAH knockdown was associated with diminished adhesion and smaller focal adhesion size as compared to cells expressing nontargeting shRNA (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: Expression of PCARE B resulted in a similar decrease in adhesion as ENAH knockdown, suggesting suppression of ENAH function at focal adhesions.
source: Intriguingly, expression of PCARE B resulted in a similar decrease in adhesion, suggesting suppression of ENAH function at focal adhesions (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: Expression of PCARE B in MCF7 cells shifted the enrichment of ENAH from focal adhesions to membrane protrusions.
source: Importantly, the expression of PCARE B in MCF7 cells shifted the enrichment of ENAH from focal adhesions to membrane protrusions (Figure 2G center inset).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: ENAH enrichment at protrusions was not observed in MCF7 cells expressing Mito-mRuby2-PCARE B, which exhibited strong mitochondrial localization of ENAH and markedly decreased adhesion.
source: ENAH enrichment at protrusions was not observed in MCF7 cells expressing Mito-mRuby2-PCARE B, which exhibited strong mitochondrial localization of ENAH and markedly decreased adhesion (Figure 2G right inset, Figure 2H,I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: The crystal structure of ENAH EVH1 domain fused to a 36-mer PCARE sequence was solved to 1.65 Å resolution.
source: To understand the structural basis for the high-affinity and selective interaction of PCARE B with ENAH, we solved a crystal structure of ENAH EVH1 domain fused to a 36-mer PCARE sequence to 1.65 Å resolution.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and methods described in the manuscript.

claim: Only 21 residues of PCARE were fully resolved in the electron density (PCARE828–848).
source: Consistent with our truncation studies, our structure showed that only 21 residues of PCARE were fully resolved in the electron density (PCARE828–848, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The LPPPP motif in PCARE binds at the expected canonical site, but in the opposite orientation from previously observed Ena/VASP EVH1 domains engaged with proline-rich peptides.
source: The high-resolution structure led to the surprising discovery that the LPPPP motif in PCARE binds at the expected canonical site, but in the opposite orientation from previously observed Ena/VASP EVH1 domains engaged with proline-rich peptides (Ball et al., 2000; Prehoda et al., 1999; Fedorov et al., 1999; Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3A, B and comparison to prior structures.

claim: PCARE828–848 uses a 14-residue alpha helix-rich extension C-terminal to the LPPPP motif to make additional contacts to an extended region on the EVH1 domain, explaining its high affinity.
source: PCARE828–848 uses a 14-residue alpha helix-rich extension C-terminal to the LPPPP motif to make additional contacts to an extended region on the EVH1 domain, explaining its high affinity.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3C and structural analysis.

claim: PCARE residues Phe843 and Leu846 make hydrophobic interactions with Ala83 and Pro65 on ENAH.
source: PCARE residues Phe843 and Leu846 make hydrophobic interactions with Ala83 and Pro65 on ENAH.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The side chain of Asp840 on PCARE docks into a polar pocket on ENAH made up of the backbone atoms of ENAH residues Lys69 and Arg81.
source: The side chain of Asp840 on PCARE docks into a polar pocket on ENAH made up of the backbone atoms of ENAH residues Lys69 and Arg81.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The backbone NH and side-chain hydroxyl group of Ser842 on PCARE form hydrogen bonds with the side chain of Asp840.
source: Notably, the backbone NH and side-chain hydroxyl group of Ser842 on PCARE form hydrogen bonds with the side chain of Asp840, positioning Asp840 to hydrogen bond with a water molecule that is further coordinated by the backbone NH of ENAH Arg81.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The alpha-helical structure of PCARE828–848 buries the smaller Val837 in the same site where phenylalanine can bind.
source: Most intriguing is the interaction between Val837 on PCARE and the hydrophobic groove in ENAH, which typically engages large aromatic residues. The alpha-helical structure of PCARE828–848 buries the smaller Val837 in the same site where phenylalanine can bind.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and structural analysis.

claim: ENAH P65D mutation led to a dramatic 100-fold weakening of the affinity of ENAH EVH1 for free PCARE B peptide.
source: However, this single mutation led to a dramatic 100-fold weakening of the affinity of ENAH EVH1 for free PCARE B peptide.
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Table 1.

claim: The ENAH P65D mutation has little effect on the binding of ActA.
source: Residue 65, shown in Figure 3C, is remote from the canonical FP4-binding site and, as expected, this mutation has little effect on the binding of ActA (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Table 1.

claim: 16 of the 18 residues that are within 4 Å of PCARE in ENAH are identical in ENAH, VASP, and EVL.
source: Interestingly, our structure of ENAH EVH1 domain bound to PCARE828–848 shows that 16 of the 18 residues that are within 4 Å of PCARE in ENAH are identical in ENAH ,VASP, and EVL.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and sequence comparison.

claim: EVL V65P bound to PCARE B fivefold weaker than did wild-type EVL (KD = 112.1 vs. 22 μM).
source: Surprisingly, EVL V65P bound to PCARE B fivefold weaker than did wild-type EVL (KD = 112.1 vs. 22 μM, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Table 1.

claim: EVL V65P bound to an FP4-containing ActA peptide with the same affinity as wild-type EVL (KD = 2.4 vs. 2.7 μM).
source: In contrast, EVL V65P bound to an FP4-containing ActA peptide, which does not contact Val65 (Barone et al., 2020), with the same affinity as wild-type EVL (KD = 2.4 vs. 2.7 μM, Table 1), indicating that the V65P mutation does not lead to global disruption of the domain structure but does influence its interaction with PCARE.
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Table 1 and citation to prior literature.

claim: Comparing the structures of ENAH EVH1 domain bound to PCARE828–848 vs. the peptide FPPPP shows a conformational difference in ENAH: a loop composed of residues 80–86 is shifted by 3 Å.
source: Comparing the structures of ENAH EVH1 domain bound to PCARE828–848 vs. the peptide FPPPP (PDB 1EVH; Prehoda et al., 1999) shows a conformational difference in ENAH: a loop composed of residues 80–86, which forms part of the extended PCARE-binding site, is shifted by 3 Å (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The EVL Y62C V65P EVH1 domain double mutant bound to PCARE B with KD = 2.2 μM, which is 10-fold lower than the KD for wild-type EVL and a striking 56-fold lower than the KD for binding to EVL V65P.
source: The Y62C mutation alone had almost no measurable effect on the binding of EVL EVH1 domain to PCARE (Table 1), but the EVL Y62C V65P EVH1 domain double mutant bound to PCARE B with KD = 2.2 μM, which is 10-fold lower than the KD for wild-type EVL and a striking 56-fold lower than the KD for binding to EVL V65P (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Table 1.

claim: The dramatic enhancement in affinity for the EVL Y62C V65P double mutant relative to either single mutant indicates strong coupling between positions 62 and 65.
source: This dramatic enhancement in affinity for the double mutant relative to either single mutant indicates strong coupling between positions 62 and 65, consistent with the rearrangement of a loop upon PCARE binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data shown in Table 1.

claim: Seven replacements of EVL residues with ENAH residues were sufficient to recapitulate dTERMen energies similar to that for ENAH in the PCARE828–848-bound conformation.
source: Seven replacements were sufficient to recapitulate dTERMen energies similar to that for ENAH in the PCARE828–848-bound conformation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by dTERMen modeling results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: EVLswapped bound as tightly to PCARE B as did ENAH EVH1 (KD = 0.35 vs. 0.32 μM).
source: We made a mutated EVL EVH1 domain with the seven corresponding residues from ENAH. This protein, EVLswapped, bound as tightly to PCARE B as did ENAH EVH1 (KD = 0.35 vs. 0.32 μM) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Peptide PCARE-Dual bound ~sevenfold tighter than PCARE B, with KD = 50 nM.
source: Peptide PCARE-Dual bound ~ sevenfold tighter than PCARE B, with KD = 50 nM (Figure 5B, D).
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Figure 5B and 5D.

claim: PCARE-Dual interacted ~eightfold less tightly with a mutant of ENAH EVH1 domain that had a Y38E substitution in the noncanonical site (KD = 0.38 ± 0.01 μM).
source: Consistent with the designed two-site binding, PCARE-Dual interacted ~ eightfold less tightly with a mutant of ENAH EVH1 domain that had a Y38E substitution in the noncanonical site (KD = 0.38 ± 0.01 μM; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ABI1–LPP fusion peptide bound with KD = 0.76 μM, which is threefold tighter than the ABI1 portion alone and fivefold tighter than the LPP portion alone.
source: The ABI1–LPP fusion peptide bound with KD = 0.76 μM, which is threefold tighter than the ABI1 portion alone and fivefold tighter than the LPP portion alone, although weaker overall than PCARE-Dual.
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PCARE-Dual dissociates ~100-fold slower than dual-motif peptide LPP.
source: The enhancements in affinity for PCARE-Dual and ABI1-LPP come from decreases in off-rate, with PCARE-Dual dissociating ~100-fold slower than dual-motif peptide LPP (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by BLI dissociation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PCARE-Dual is 400- to 600-fold selective for ENAH over EVL and VASP.
source: Finally, we found that PCARE-Dual is 400- to 600-fold selective for ENAH over EVL and VASP, even though VASP is also known to have a noncanonical binding site that can engage a second FP4 motif (Acevedo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Figure 5D and citation to prior literature.

claim: The dual-motif peptides provide the tightest and most specific known binders to the ENAH EVH1 domain to date.
source: To our knowledge, our dual-motif peptides provide the tightest and most specific known binders to the ENAH EVH1 domain to date (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on comparison of binding data to known literature and supported by data in Figure 5D.

claim: Synthetic mini-protein pGolemi binds to ENAH with KD = 0.29 μM, moderate selectivity (20-fold) over VASP, and higher selectivity (≥120-fold) over EVL.
source: Synthetic mini-protein pGolemi binds to ENAH with KD = 0.29 μM, moderate selectivity (20-fold) over VASP, and higher selectivity (≥120-fold) over EVL (Golemi-Kotra et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The mechanism behind the specificity of pGolemi has not been determined.
source: The mechanism behind the specificity of pGolemi has not been determined, and mutational data do not readily rationalize a model (Holtzman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Both ENAH and VASP have been identified in affinity purification-mass spectrometry experiments using PCARE as bait in ciliated cells.
source: Both ENAH and VASP have been identified in affinity purification-mass spectrometry experiments using PCARE as bait in ciliated cells (Corral-Serrano et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ENAH and VASP can heterotetramerize.
source: Given that ENAH and VASP can heterotetramerize, VASP may be recruited to the identified complexes indirectly, via interaction with ENAH (Gertler et al., 1996; Riquelme et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: VASP may be recruited to PCARE-containing complexes indirectly, via interaction with ENAH.
source: Given that ENAH and VASP can heterotetramerize, VASP may be recruited to the identified complexes indirectly, via interaction with ENAH (Gertler et al., 1996; Riquelme et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of ENAH and VASP to heterotetramerize and the specificity of PCARE for ENAH.

claim: The PPII helix possesses twofold rotational pseudosymmetry, meaning that the side chains and backbone carbonyls are similarly positioned in either the N-to-C- or C-to-N-terminal directions.
source: The PPII helix possesses twofold rotational pseudosymmetry, meaning that the side chains and backbone carbonyls are similarly positioned in either the N-to-C- or C-to-N-terminal directions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PPII helix structure.

claim: SH3 domains exploit the pseudosymmetry of PPII helices to bind proline-rich sequences in either direction.
source: SH3 domains exploit this pseudosymmetry to bind proline-rich sequences in either direction (Zarrinpar et al., 2003a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: All Ena/VASP and Homer EVH1 domain structures solved so far show the PPII helix engaged in a single direction.
source: Although all Ena/VASP and Homer EVH1 domain structures solved so far show the PPII helix engaged in a single direction, the WASP EVH1 domain binds its proline-rich ligand in the opposite direction (Volkman et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of prior structural studies and supported by a citation.

claim: The WASP EVH1 domain binds its proline-rich ligand in the opposite direction from Ena/VASP and Homer EVH1 domains.
source: Although all Ena/VASP and Homer EVH1 domain structures solved so far show the PPII helix engaged in a single direction, the WASP EVH1 domain binds its proline-rich ligand in the opposite direction (Volkman et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: It has long been hypothesized, although never demonstrated, that Ena/VASP EVH1 domains might also bind FP4 motifs in either direction.
source: Consequently, it has long been hypothesized, although never demonstrated, that Ena/VASP EVH1 domains might also bind FP4 motifs in either direction (Ball et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The large effect on PCARE binding observed for EVL V65P compared to wild-type EVL EVH1 suggests that EVL also binds PCARE in a reversed orientation.
source: Interestingly, the large effect on PCARE binding that we observed for EVL V65P compared to wild-type EVL EVH1 suggests that EVL also binds PCARE in a reversed orientation (relative to FP4 ligands such as ActA), albeit weakly, because this is the orientation that best explains contacts with position 65.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data in Table 1 and structural analysis.

claim: The cancer drug Gleevec achieves 3000-fold selectivity for Abl over Src, despite the fact that the two proteins share ~46% sequence identity across the kinase domain, and ~86% identity in the Gleevec-binding site.
source: However, this mechanism is reminiscent of how the cancer drug Gleevec achieves 3000-fold selectivity for Abl over Src, despite the fact that the two proteins share ~46 % sequence identity across the kinase domain, and ~86 % identity in the Gleevec-binding site (Seeliger et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A few residue swaps based on sequence alignments and structure gazing failed to rescue the affinity of Src for Gleevec, because these mutations failed to account for the higher-order epistatic interactions that contribute to specificity.
source: As we found here, a few residue swaps based on sequence alignments and structure gazing failed to rescue the affinity of Src for Gleevec, because these mutations failed to account for the higher-order epistatic interactions that contribute to specificity (Seeliger et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Retracing the evolutionary trajectories that led to extant Src and Abl kinases, using ancestral reconstruction, allowed identification of residues involved in a hydrogen-bonding network distant from the Gleevec-binding interface that are key for selective binding to Abl.
source: Interestingly, because evolution has sampled kinase sequence space under the constraints of epistasis, retracing the evolutionary trajectories that led to extant Src and Abl kinases, using ancestral reconstruction, allowed Wilson et al. to identify residues involved in a hydrogen-bonding network distant from the Gleevec-binding interface that are key for selective binding to Abl (Wilson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Randomizing hydrophobic core residues of the SH3 domain from human Fyn tyrosine kinase could effectively switch its affinity and specificity to different ligands.
source: A recent study demonstrated that randomizing hydrophobic core residues of the SH3 domain from human Fyn tyrosine kinase could effectively switch its affinity and specificity to different ligands (Ben-David et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Directed evolution experiments that varied only the hydrophobic core residues of ubiquitin yielded a conformationally stabilized ubiquitin variant that was specific for the deubiquitinase USP7.
source: In addition, directed evolution experiments that varied only the hydrophobic core residues of ubiquitin yielded a conformationally stabilized ubiquitin variant that was specific for the deubiquitinase USP7 (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Cytoplasmic expression of a PCARE peptide displaces ENAH from focal adhesions but not membrane protrusions.
source: Cytoplasmic expression of a PCARE peptide displaces ENAH from focal adhesions but not membrane protrusions, indicating that this peptide could serve as a valuable tool to selectively perturb EVH1-dependent functions of ENAH.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: A mito-tagged PCARE peptide selectively sequesters ENAH at the mitochondria, depleting it from sites of normal function and inhibiting ENAH-dependent biological processes such as cell adhesion.
source: In contrast, a mito-tagged PCARE peptide selectively sequesters ENAH at the mitochondria, depleting it from sites of normal function and inhibiting ENAH-dependent biological processes such as cell adhesion.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2D-I.

claim: The high avidity of PCARE peptides when localized to the mitochondrial surface could potentially outcompete interactions between the EVH2 domain of ENAH and actin-based structures.
source: This is likely due to the high avidity of these peptides when localized to the mitochondrial surface, which could potentially outcompete interactions between the EVH2 domain of ENAH and actin-based structures (Bachmann et al., 1999).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed effects and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ENAH, but not VASP or EVL, is a regulator of local translation in neurons.
source: For example, ENAH, but not VASP or EVL, is a regulator of local translation in neurons (Vidaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: EVL has a specific role in durotactic invasion.
source: In contrast, EVL has a specific role in durotactic invasion (Puleo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: VASP is phosphorylated at Tyr39 by c-Abl.
source: Interestingly, although VASP is phosphorylated at Tyr39 by c-Abl, we did not find direct evidence in the literature for corresponding phosphorylation of ENAH at the analogous position Tyr38 (Maruoka et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ENAH is a substrate of c-Abl, but the ENAH modification site is Tyr 296.
source: ENAH is a substrate of c-Abl, but experiments by Tani et al. using transfected murine ENAH or ENAH mutants, c-Abl, and the adapter protein Abi1 showed that the ENAH modification site is Tyr 296; the mutation Y296F ablated the phosphorylation signal, indicating that Y38 is not a site of modification, at least under the tested conditions (Tani et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Extensive structure-based design and chemical optimization recently led to a high-affinity molecule (KD = 120 nM) that reduced breast cancer cell extravasation in a zebrafish model.
source: The role of ENAH in cancer metastasis has motivated work to identify inhibitors of its EVH1-mediated interactions, and extensive structure-based design and chemical optimization recently led to a high-affinity molecule (KD = 120 nM) that reduced breast cancer cell extravasation in a zebrafish model.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of recent work in the field.

claim: The recently developed high-affinity inhibitor has similar affinity for ENAH, EVL, and VASP because it binds to the highly conserved FP4-binding site.
source: However, because the molecule binds to the highly conserved FP4-binding site, this inhibitor has similar affinity for ENAH, EVL, and VASP (Barone et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ENAH deficiency in mouse models of cancer has been shown to decrease metastasis by reducing tumor cell invasion and intravasation.
source: ENAH deficiency in mouse models of cancer has been shown to decrease metastasis by reducing tumor cell invasion and intravasation (Roussos et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: EVL is known to promote the formation of cortical actin bundles that suppress the invasion of breast cancer cells.
source: On the other hand, EVL is known to promote the formation of cortical actin bundles that suppress the invasion of breast cancer cells (Padilla-Rodriguez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.
